events.title: UNICEF Somalia Humanitarian Situation Report No.3, 1 July - 30 September 2026
events.summary: Country: Somalia Source: UN Children's Fund Please refer to the attached file. Highlights Somalia's humanitarian needs remained high during the quarter, driven by drought, conflict, displacement, disease outbreaks and declining humanitarian assistance. An estimated 5.1 million people faced acute food insecurity (IPC Phase 3+), while 1.92 million children were projected to suffer acute malnutrition between July 2026 and June 2027. About 75,000 displacement movements and over 1,400 conflict events were recorded. UNICEF sustained lifesaving assistance across priority sectors, reaching 98,241 children with SAM treatment, 244,022 caregivers with IYCF counselling, 145,671 people with primary health care, and 286,006 people with safe water. Education support benefited 71,644 children, while 48,991 people accessed child protection services. Monthly cash transfers supported 13,493 vulnerable women, strengthening household resilience. The 2026 Humanitarian Action for Children (HAC) appeal was 27 per cent funded (US$32 million) against US$121 million required, leaving a US$89 million gap. Underfunding continued to constrain service coverage, operational capacity and emergency preparedness for anticipated El Nino impacts.

Les enfants souffrent de manière disproportionnée durant les conflits. Leurs petits corps, en plein développement, sont particulièrement vulnérables aux conséquences des armes explosives. Leurs esprits, qui forgent encore leur image d’eux-mêmes, leur sentiment de sécurité et leur compréhension du monde, vivent différemment les traumatismes, avec des effets potentiellement durables sur leur développement. events.summary: Country: World Source: Peace Research Institute Oslo Please refer to the attached file. More children than ever live in conflict zones Posted Thursday, 19 Nov 2026 by Gudrun Østby & Siri Aas Rustad More children now live near armed conflict than the combined populations of the United States, Canada and Mexico. Armed violence escalated sharply across the globe in 2025. Data from the Uppsala Conflict Data Program (UCDP) shows that conflict-related fatalities rose to 244,600, up from approximately 187,000 in 2024. This made 2025 one of the deadliest years since the end of the Cold War. Much of the increase was driven by a dramatic rise in violence targeting civilians, particularly in Sudan. While armed conflict affects entire populations, children are among those who suffer the most severe and lasting consequences. Children face grave violations , including killing and maiming, recruitment by armed groups, sexual violence, abduction, attacks on schools and hospitals, and denial of humanitarian access. But the consequences of war extend far beyond direct violence. Children living in conflict-affected areas are more likely to drop out of school, lack access to clean water, and face heightened risks of death from illness, malnutrition, or lack of vaccines and medical care. Today, Save the Children launches its new report, Stop the War on Children 2026 . The report is based on PRIO’s tenth annual mapping of children in armed conflict covering the period 1990–2025. Our latest estimates show that 589 million children, more than one in five of the world's children, were living in conflict zones in 2025 . events.title: oPt: Beyond Compliance: Strengthening Environmental, Social, Governance and Technical Assurance in Fragile Contexts for Accountable Delivery and Sustainable Impact (Project Insight Note #17)
events.summary: Country: occupied Palestinian territory Source: International Water Management Institute Please refer to the attached file. Wasudha Abeyrathna, Umar Liaqat, Stephen Fragaszy, Vidhisha Samarasekara Abstract/Description This Project Insight Note (PIN) shares lessons from the Al Murunah project’s pilot in Palestine, led by the International Water Management Institute (IWMI) and implemented with the Palestinian Hydrology Group (PHG), on strengthening environmental, social and governance (ESG) and technical assurance for physical works in fragile and conflict-affected settings. It describes a layered assurance approach that includes early partner due diligence, a living ESG risk register, multidisciplinary technical and safeguards reviews, quantity and cost verification, virtual field trips, and an independent engineering review when site access was lost. The PIN shows that ESG oversight works best when it is built into project design and followed through with corrective action and sustainability planning, helping to build trust and support the scaling of climate resilience investment.

The figure represents an increase of more than 50% in a decade, jumping from 378 million in 2015 to 589 million in 2025, according to the report Stop the War on Children: Changing the Odds , which draws on data from the Peace Research Institute Oslo (PRIO). The report found that the share of the world’s children living in conflict zones more than doubled from about 10% in the mid-1990s to 23.4% in 2025. Africa is home to the highest number of children living in conflict zones, accounting for about 260 million, or 44% of the global total. This is nearly a 20% increase from the 218 million children in Africa who lived in conflict zones in 2024. Across Africa, the proportion of children living in conflict zones more than tripled from about one in eight children in 2010 to about two in five in 2025, the highest level ever recorded for the continent. This puts Africa on par with the Middle East, where both regions now have two in five children living in conflict zones. Elsewhere, about one in four children (24.2%) in the Americas lived in conflict zones in 2025, one in seven (14.3%) in Asia, and nearly one in nine (10.6%) in Europe. events.title: World: Oxfam reaction to the inadequate pledges to the Adaptation Fund High-Level Contributor Dialogue
events.summary: Country: World Source: Oxfam Reacting to the inadequate pledges to the Adaptation Fund High-Level Contributor Dialogue, Nafkote Dabi, Climate Change Policy and Advocacy Lead said: “For the third year in a row, rich countries have failed to meet the modest $300 million Adaptation Fund target, which is just 0.1 percent of the $300 billion Global South countries need to adapt to a crisis they did little to create. We’re being told there is no money, but taxing luxury carbon – from private jets to the excess profits of fossil fuel corporations – could raise over $445 billion a year. So, let’s stop pretending this is about money. It’s about political choices, priorities, and accountability. With communities from Nepal to the Sahel being battered by escalating climate disasters, the solution is simple: make rich polluters pay.” Notes to editors Contributors announced pledges totaling just $50 million. The Adaptation Fund is the only UNFCCC-linked fund dedicated to providing grant-based adaptation finance to low- and middle-income OR Global South countries, which is the only fair and just method of delivering climate finance. At COP29, a new goal was set to reach at least $300 billion per year by 2035. A year later, it was further agreed to (within the $300 billion target) triple support for adaptation by 2035. Global South countries believe the tripling must be a tripling by 2035 of the already agreed doubling by 2025 compared to 2019 levels, leading to at least $120 billion a year by 2035. Ukrainian civil society organisations working with several international donors often undergo a separate due diligence assessment for each partner. Donors frequently request the same documents and review the same aspects of an organisation’s work, yet organisations cannot always use the results of an earlier assessment in a subsequent one. events.title: World: How AI is helping to reinforce polio surveillance in Africa
events.summary: Country: World Source: Global Polio Eradication Initiative **Brazzaville—** Every week, the polio eradication programme at the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa receives surveillance and operational data from the region’s 47 countries. From poliovirus detections and laboratory results to vaccination campaign coverage and health facility visits, this information is essential to guiding outbreak response and reaching every child. But with growing volumes of data spread across different platforms, turning information into actionable insights has not always been straightforward. Until recently, producing a district-level map or country summary often involved several manual steps: locating datasets, cleaning and combining information, and generating maps, charts and reports. During an outbreak, teams could spend valuable time waiting for an analyst to provide the information they needed to make decisions. The WHO Africa’s Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Centre is changing this through the integration of AI into its operational dashboards. Instead of navigating multiple databases or relying on technical expertise, programme officers can now ask questions in plain language and receive relevant maps, charts or tables directly from the dashboards. For example, an officer can request a breakdown of circulating variant poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) detections by district in a specific country since January 2026. The system retrieves the relevant information and presents it in an accessible visual format, allowing users to explore trends by location, reporting period or virus type. The Poliovirus Detection Dashboard also features an AI-powered query function that generates written summaries from current and archived records, supported by relevant figures.

events.title: Apec summit live: Xi and Putin start talks as Trump arrives in China
events.summary: Summit in Chinese tech hub Shenzhen set to include highly anticipated meeting between Xi, Trump and Putin Shenzhen takes centre stage as Xi sends ‘Chinamaxxing’ message at Apec summit What is Apec? Explained in 30 seconds Yalta became a byword for betrayal. Will Trump, Xi and Putin enact another carve-up? That is the question the Guardian’s diplomatic correspondent Patrick Wintour seeks to address in his piece about the expected, Putin, Trump and Xi, meeting at Apec on Thursday. It is a truism in diplomacy that if you are not around the table, the risk is that you, or your values, are on the menu and about to be carved up. Many excluded from the summit in Shenzhen, principally Ukraine but also eastern Europe and Baltic countries, Taiwan and even Iran, have reason to be nervous that their sponsors might abandon them in a complex geopolitical trade-off that Putin envisions, and Trump seems to endorse.
